newsitem.title: USA: Russia sticks to IMF loan conditions-Yasin.
newsitem.headline: Russia sticks to IMF loan conditions-Yasin.

text.p: Russia is sticking to the conditions set out in its $10 billion International Monetary Fund loan program and will continue to do so, Economy Minister Yevgeny Yasin said on Tuesday.

Asked about talks with Fund leaders held during this week's IMF-World Bank annual meetings, Yasin said, "we were able to state that the basic conditions of this program are fundamentally being fulfilled."
Yasin said Fund officials had congratulated Russian ministers on economic successes, especially lowering inflation.
Yasin said Russia's monthly inflation rate was 0.3 percent in September after a 0.2 percent fall in prices in August.
He said prices usually rise in October and November. "Evidently, we will see that, but I do not expect inflation to exceed one percent," he said.
Yasin also said Russia supported an initiative to reduce the debt of some of the world's poorest countries but could not join in the plan unless it was admitted to the Paris Club of creditor states.
"We are prepared to adhere to these conditions but for them to be equally and mutually beneficial, Russia must be a member of the Paris Club," Yasin said.
Russia earlier this year reached agreement with the IMF on a three-year Extended Fund Facility loan but it is subject to strict monthly monitoring.
Russia must meet certain monetary targets, which incldue the budget deficit and net reserves.
Yasin said it could be difficult to meet the reserves target as it was sometimes necessary to use them to support the rouble, which is in a crawling peg against the dollar.

Central bank chairman Sergei Dubinin said last month that Russia spent $1.6 billion to support the rouble, when a faster than usual decline against the dollar made short-term Treasury bilol yields unattractive..
However, Yasin said Russia could meet the IMF conditions.
"On the whole I think we will be able to," he said.
A tranche of $330 million was held up in August because of concern over the low level of tax collection and Russian officials acknowledge the revenue side of the budget is a difficult problem.
Yasin said the tax and revenue issue had been discussed during the talks with the IMF.
"Of course they expressed anxiety but it was recognised that the government is working very energetically to resolve these problems," he said.

The International Monetary Fund and World Bank this week launched an initiative to offer poor, heavily indebted states relief on up to 80 percent of their debts, against the 67 percent relief currently on offer.
Yasin said Russia, which inherited the debts and assets of the former Soviet Union, was owed $140 billion. This exceeded the money it owed to, among others, the Paris Club.
Russia wasnts all debts it is owed, including credits to buy military equipment, recognised and wants them to reflect the exchange rate at the time they were granted.
Yasin said Russia was excluded from talks with some debtor states as it was not a member of the Paris Club.
Many of Russia's debtors are African countries which were granted credits, often at artificially low rates, but are now unable to repay them.
Russia has reached an agreement on rescheduling its own debts to the Paris Club and has been pressing for admission as a creditor.
--Nigel Stephenson, Washington newsroom +1 202 898 8329
